 FAIR Urges Supreme Court to Unblock Wall
 FAIR Urges Supreme Court to Unblock Wall
 November 5, 2026 
 Shows lower-court injunction should be suspended 
 WASHINGTON—The Federation for American Immigration Reform (FAIR) has filed a brief in the U.S. Supreme Court urging it to suspend an injunction by the U.S. District Court for the Western District of Texas. The injunction blocks the federal government from waiving environmental and other requirements that would otherwise stand in the way of border wall construction in the Big Bend sector of the U.S.-Mexico border.
 As FAIR shows in its brief, the courts lack jurisdiction to review such waivers and thereby block wall construction, unless there has been a violation of the Constitution. Here, the district court purported to base its injunction on a violation of the major questions doctrine, which it claimed is a constitutional doctrine.
 As FAIR explains, however, the major questions doctrine is a Supreme Court-made rule against complicated statutory interpretations giving agencies vast new powers that were likely not foreseen or intended by Congress. It is not a constitutional doctrine. Even if it were, it does not even apply to this case, where the only statutory issue is the simple one of whether the illegal entries through the Big Bend sector have been, as the waiver provision requires, “high.”
 “To some district courts, any meritless argument is good enough to delay strong enforcement policies,” said Christopher J. Hajec, deputy general counsel of FAIR. “The Court should see through the tissue paper-thin excuse for this delay of the border wall’s completion, suspend the lower court’s injunction, and let the wall be built while this case continues.”
 The case is Mullin v. Friends of the Ruidosa Church , No. 26A560 (Supreme Court).
 To read the brief click here .

 Immigration Term
 Immigration and Nationality Act (INA)
 This Act of October 3, 1965 abolished national origin and race as criteria restricting for immigration to the United States, and replaced this national origins quota system with a first-come, first served basis, with preference for relatives of U.S. citizens and for people with special occupational skills needed in the U.S. It also established the category of immediate relatives as numerically unrestricted.
